lessons.title: TCP congestion control with BBR: model the bottleneck instead of waiting for loss
lessons.mechanism: Global FortiOS TCP sender congestion-control selection between default CUBIC and model-based BBR using bottleneck bandwidth and propagation RTT.
lessons.workflow: TCP sender pacing -> bottleneck bandwidth/RTT model -> ACK-derived delivery feedback -> pacing/cwnd adjustment; configured globally rather than per firewall policy.
lessons.failure: Low TCP goodput on a congested or high-RTT path; a policy-only change is incorrectly expected to alter the global TCP algorithm.
lessons.evidence: config system global read-back proves selected algorithm; controlled same-path transfer plus RTT/loss/retransmission measurements tests outcome; neither alone proves an application is healthy.
lessons.remediation: A/B test CUBIC and BBR under identical path, policy, endpoints and load; change globally in a controlled window; revert to CUBIC if fairness or stability regresses.
lessons.diagram: Closed-loop sender/bottleneck/ACK feedback with BBR bandwidth-RTT estimator and pacing controller.
lessons.content_html:
FortiOS 8.0 adds BBR as an alternative TCP congestion-control algorithm. CUBIC remains the default. The important engineering distinction is that this is a TCP sender-control choice, not a route-selection algorithm, an SD-WAN SLA, or a firewall-policy action. It changes how the FortiGate controls the rate at which TCP data is injected into a path. That matters when the limiting factor is a congested bottleneck and the path has meaningful round-trip delay: a loss-driven algorithm can reduce its sending rate after congestion loss even when the path could still carry more data, while BBR builds a model of bottleneck bandwidth and propagation RTT and uses that model to pace traffic.

Mechanics and packet-flow implications

BBR estimates two path properties from delivery feedback: the rate at which the bottleneck can deliver data and the minimum round-trip propagation time that represents the path without queueing. Their product is a bandwidth-delay estimate of the amount of data that can be in flight. BBR uses pacing to approach that delivery rate rather than relying only on loss-triggered congestion-window reduction. CUBIC uses a cubic window-growth function and remains the default selection. Neither algorithm removes physical loss, repairs a bad queue, or increases the capacity of the circuit. The result depends on where the bottleneck sits, how the remote TCP stack behaves, whether inspection is CPU-bound, and whether a shaper or provider policer is already imposing a lower rate.

The Fortinet example is deliberately controlled: create a proxy-mode firewall policy, enable UTM, use the default antivirus profile and certificate-inspection SSL profile, set CUBIC, then download a 100 MB object across a path configured with 50 ms delay and 1% packet loss. Repeat with BBR under the same conditions. The proxy-mode policy is part of the documented test setup; do not silently change inspection mode, security profiles, endpoints, or traffic shaping between runs, because those changes confound the comparison.

Configuration and verification

config system global
    set tcp-congestion-control bbr
end

# Restore the default algorithm
config system global
    set tcp-congestion-control cubic
end

The setting is global. Do not look for a per-policy or per-interface BBR toggle. Read back the system-global configuration after the change and record the FortiOS build. Then run repeated transfers with the same source, destination, object size, policy, inspection profile, shaping and path impairment. Measure application goodput, RTT, retransmissions and CPU at the same time. A single successful HTTP 200 response proves the application transaction completed; it does not prove that BBR increased throughput. A configuration read-back proves the algorithm selection; it does not prove that the path is congestion-limited.

Operational diagnosis

If throughput is poor, first determine whether the sender is actually congestion-limited. Compare interface utilization, FortiGate CPU, policy counters, shaping counters, server-side throughput and packet captures. If the link is not full but retransmissions and RTT rise under load, congestion control is a plausible experiment. If the firewall is CPU-bound by proxy inspection, the WAN is rate-limited below the BBR pacing rate, or the server is the bottleneck, changing BBR may produce little or no improvement. If only one direction changes, test which endpoint is the TCP sender in that direction; the algorithm is not a symmetric path-quality setting.

BBR is not a universal “faster” switch. It is a system-wide behavior change and can alter how FortiGate TCP flows compete with other senders. Roll it out to a representative traffic class only after a controlled lab comparison, but remember that the knob itself is global. Establish a rollback threshold for retransmissions, latency under load, application completion time and fairness before changing production. The practical implication is simple: use BBR when measured TCP congestion is the problem, not as a substitute for fixing a saturated circuit, poor QoS, an overloaded inspection path, or an unhealthy application server.

lessons.title: TPM-backed private-data encryption: the key hierarchy and the hardware-bound backup
lessons.mechanism: TPM protects the 32-hex master-encryption-password; that password derives a primary key used to encrypt individual FortiManager secrets.
lessons.workflow: Enable private-data-encryption -> enter master key -> TPM protects key material -> primary key encrypts stored credentials -> backup binds protected key to appliance.
lessons.failure: Restore or migration fails because the destination TPM/master-encryption-password does not match the encrypted backup; TPM is mistaken for disk encryption.
lessons.evidence: diagnose hardware info reports TPM detected/enabled, not the integrity of every encrypted object; successful restore with matching key validates backup compatibility.
lessons.remediation: Confirm supported hardware and TPM state, escrow the master key securely, retain tested backups, and use the correct key during restore or migration.
lessons.diagram: TPM/key hierarchy with master password, derived primary key, encrypted secrets and hardware-bound backup/restore path.
lessons.content_html:
FortiManager 8.0.0 documents TPM support on selected hardware appliances. The TPM is not a general-purpose disk-encryption feature. Its job is to protect the master-encryption-password used by FortiManager's private-data-encryption feature. That distinction matters during incident response and hardware replacement: a device can report that a TPM is present while the administrator still misunderstands what data is protected, or a backup can be perfectly intact yet impossible to restore because the key context does not match.

Key hierarchy and what is stored where

Private data encryption is disabled by default. When enabled, FortiManager requires a 32-hexadecimal-digit master-encryption-password. FortiManager uses AES-128-CBC to encrypt sensitive data. The TPM generates a 2048-bit primary key that protects the master-encryption-password with RSA-2048; the master-encryption-password protects the data, while the primary key protects the master password. The primary key encrypts individual passwords stored by FortiManager, including administrator, HA and SNMP passwords. The individual passwords are not each stored inside the TPM. The primary key is not displayed in the backup file or system CLI; the TPM protects the master-encryption-password/key relationship so the encrypted credential material is not exposed as readable configuration.

FortiManager 8.0.0 lists supported hardware models including FMG-200G, FMG-400G, FMG-410G, FMG-1000G, FMG-3100G, FMG-3700G and FMG-3750G. Model support is release-specific; verify the exact model and release notes before planning a hardware refresh. A VM or an unsupported appliance must not be assumed to have the same TPM behavior.

Enablement and evidence

diagnose hardware info

config system global
    set private-data-encryption enable
end

When private-data-encryption is enabled, the CLI prompts for the 32-hexadecimal-digit key and asks for it again. Treat that value as a recovery secret: store it in an approved enterprise vault, restrict access, and test the documented recovery process. The diagnose hardware info output includes a TPM information section. “Detected/enabled” proves that the hardware module is available to FortiManager; “not detected/disabled” or “not available” identifies a hardware or enablement boundary. It does not prove that every stored secret has been encrypted correctly, that a backup is recoverable, or that the managed FortiGate configuration database is protected.

Backup, restore and migration behavior

The primary key binds an encrypted backup to a particular FortiManager unit and does not leave the TPM. During backup, the TPM protects the master-encryption-password in the backup. During restore, a TPM-enabled destination with a different master-encryption-password cannot restore that configuration. A destination with the same password can restore it. The master-encryption-password is also required when migrating the configuration even if the destination model does not have a TPM. Therefore, a hardware replacement plan must include the correct key and a supported restore path before the source unit is retired.

Do not infer that TPM encrypts the FortiManager disk drive. Fortinet's Administration Guide states that TPM does not encrypt the FortiManager disk drive. Treat the Device Manager database and managed-device configuration data as a separate storage-protection concern; TPM is not a substitute for disk, backup, access-control and database protection. The same guide states that every HA cluster member must use the same master-encryption-key for the cluster to form and synchronize; verify this requirement against the exact 8.0 build before a hardware or HA migration. Do not publish the master key in automation logs or commit it to a Git repository.

Failure isolation

If a restore fails, separate three questions: is the model supported, is the TPM detected and enabled, and does the destination have the same master-encryption-password as the backup? A TPM status line answers only the second question. If the backup is from a TPM-enabled unit and the destination key differs, repeatedly retrying the restore will not fix the mismatch. Recover the escrowed key or use the documented migration procedure. A successful restore with the expected key proves the key/backup relationship worked; it does not establish that every managed-device configuration is encrypted at rest. The operational lesson is to treat TPM enablement as a lifecycle decision: key escrow, backup testing, hardware compatibility and restore ownership must be designed before enabling it in production.

lessons.title: ADOM lifecycle and device modes: why disabling the feature is a migration
lessons.mechanism: ADOM feature state partitions Device Manager, FortiView, logs, incidents and reports; Normal mode assigns a FortiGate as one device to one ADOM, Advanced mode allows VDOM-level assignment.
lessons.workflow: Enable as super user -> create ADOMs and assign devices/admins -> optionally assign individual VDOMs in Advanced mode -> consolidate to root and delete non-root ADOMs before disabling.
lessons.failure: ADOM disable or Advanced-to-Normal transition is blocked because non-root ADOMs or VDOM assignments remain; FortiMail/FortiWeb logging is unavailable if ADOMs are off.
lessons.evidence: ADOM/device/VDOM assignment views and the System Information Administrative Domain switch show state; they do not prove historical log data was migrated.
lessons.remediation: Inventory devices, VDOMs, administrators, report scope and retention before migration; move devices to root, delete non-root ADOMs, then disable.
lessons.diagram: ADOM state machine with root/non-root ADOMs and Normal/Advanced VDOM assignment branches.
lessons.content_html:
Administrative Domains are a FortiAnalyzer tenancy and data-organization boundary, not merely a cosmetic folder. When ADOMs are enabled, Device Manager, FortiView, Log View, Incidents & Alerts and Reports are presented per ADOM, and the administrator selects an ADOM when logging in. Only a super-user administrator can enable or configure the feature. FortiMail and FortiWeb logging and reporting require ADOMs; FortiGate and FortiCarrier devices cannot be grouped in the same ADOM, and FortiCarrier devices use their own default ADOM.

Normal and Advanced device modes

Normal is the default device mode. A FortiGate unit is added to one ADOM as a device; you cannot distribute different VDOMs from that unit across multiple ADOMs. Advanced mode allows a VDOM from one FortiGate to be assigned to a different ADOM. This can provide per-VDOM analysis and delegated administration, but it increases operational complexity because a single physical FortiGate now has several ADOM-scoped representations. FortiAnalyzer does not support splitting VDOMs from one device across ADOMs that use different device modes. Before changing Advanced back to Normal, ensure that no FortiGate VDOMs remain assigned to an ADOM.

The mode control is under System Settings > Advanced > Misc Settings in the 8.0 guide. Select Normal or Advanced in the ADOM Mode field and apply. In Advanced mode, the Device Manager behavior also differs in Workspace mode: managed-device database changes are automatically saved and applied, and the Save button is not selectable. This is an operationally important difference for change control; do not assume the same save/commit workflow that operators use in a Normal-mode deployment.

Enabling and disabling the feature

ADOMs are disabled by default. FortiAnalyzer's CLI reference also notes that enabling ADOMs moves non-global configuration items into the root ADOM, so back up the unit configuration before enabling the feature. To enable them, log in as a super user, open Dashboards > Status, and turn on Administrative Domain in the System Information widget. FortiAnalyzer logs the administrator out and returns to the login screen. After reauthentication, ADOM-scoped panes appear. Plan the ADOM hierarchy, device types, administrator assignments, report scope and retention before moving devices; enabling the feature changes how operators select and work with data.

Disabling ADOMs is deliberately a migration, not a single toggle. First remove every device from every non-root ADOM by adding it to the root ADOM. Then delete all non-root ADOMs. Only after no non-root ADOM remains can the Administrative Domain switch be turned off. FortiAnalyzer logs the administrator out again. A failed disable attempt is therefore useful evidence: it usually means a non-root ADOM or managed device still exists, not that the GUI toggle is broken.

Operational verification and troubleshooting

config system global
    set adom-status enable
    set adom-mode advanced
end

The CLI reference exposes adom-status and adom-mode; use the GUI to create and manage the ADOMs themselves. Before a change, export an inventory of ADOMs, device assignments, FortiGate VDOM assignments, administrator profiles and report dependencies. In Advanced mode, inspect VDOM membership rather than counting only physical devices. After moving a device to root, verify its logs and reports in the root ADOM and confirm that the non-root ADOM is empty before deleting it. A visible device in the root tree proves assignment; it does not prove that old logs or report definitions were merged into the new scope. Validate historical log access and report output separately.

If FortiMail or FortiWeb logging is expected, do not disable ADOMs as a cleanup exercise: the product guide explicitly requires ADOMs for those workflows. If a mode change is blocked, identify remaining VDOM-to-ADOM assignments. If a user sees different panes after the change, confirm which ADOM they selected at login and the administrator's ADOM permissions. The safe design decision is to choose Normal mode unless per-VDOM analysis is a real requirement, and to treat a transition back to Normal or to ADOM-disabled operation as a data-ownership and reporting migration with an explicit validation plan.

lessons.title: DNS over TLS on FortiSwitch: encrypted resolver traffic is not the same as authenticated DNS
lessons.mechanism: FortiSwitchOS 8.0 resolver protocol changes from default cleartext DNS to DNS over TLS on TCP/853; optional server-ca-cert enables CA validation before connection.
lessons.workflow: Switch management-plane resolver selects primary/secondary server -> TCP/853 TLS handshake -> optional CA-chain validation -> encrypted DNS query/response -> local resolver cache.
lessons.failure: Resolver timeout or TLS handshake failure after switching protocol; DoT is enabled but certificate trust is not configured, or source-IP routing/firewall blocks TCP/853.
lessons.evidence: show system dns proves protocol/server/CA settings; packet capture showing TCP/853 and TLS proves transport; it does not prove the answer is authoritative or DNSSEC-validated.
lessons.remediation: Confirm resolver DoT support, TCP/853 reachability, source IP route, CA chain and server certificate; configure server-ca-cert and test name resolution before rollout.
lessons.diagram: FortiSwitch management resolver to TLS 853 server, CA validation gate and encrypted query/response path.
lessons.content_html:
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0 adds DNS over TLS (DoT) for switch-originated resolver traffic. DoT encapsulates DNS queries and responses in TLS and uses TCP port 853. All FortiSwitch models support the feature in this release. The important default is that FortiSwitchOS continues to use cleartext DNS unless the protocol is changed. This is a management-plane resolver setting; it does not automatically encrypt DNS queries generated by every endpoint connected to the switch.

Transport and trust are separate controls

DoT protects DNS data in transit against passive observation and in-path manipulation. FortiSwitchOS can also validate the DNS server's certificate when a CA certificate is configured. The distinction is explicit in the guide: if server-ca-cert is not specified, FortiSwitchOS does not perform CA certificate validation before establishing the connection. Therefore, “DoT is enabled” means the resolver uses TLS; it does not by itself prove that the switch authenticated the intended resolver. For a managed environment, configure a trusted CA certificate and verify the server certificate chain rather than treating encryption alone as server identity.

Configuration

config system dns
    set primary 10.105.142.113
    set secondary 10.105.142.114
    set protocol dot
    set server-ca-cert "CA_Cert_1.cer"
    set source-ip 0.0.0.0
    set dns-cache-limit 2
    set dns-cache-ttl 1800
    set cache-notfound-responses disable
end

The documented cleartext selection is set protocol cleartext; DoT is set protocol dot. The resolver configuration also exposes primary and secondary servers, source IP, cache size, cache TTL and whether negative responses are cached. Those parameters are operationally relevant: a correct TLS handshake does not help if the configured source IP has no route to the resolver, the secondary server does not support DoT, or a stale cache masks a changed answer during testing.

Verification and evidence boundaries

Read back config system dns and confirm the protocol, CA object, resolver addresses and source IP. At the network boundary, a capture should show TCP connection attempts to the resolver on port 853 followed by a TLS handshake and encrypted application data. A SYN with no SYN/ACK points to reachability or firewall policy. A completed TCP handshake followed by a TLS alert suggests protocol or certificate negotiation. A successful TLS session followed by resolution failure shifts attention to the upstream resolver, DNS view, cache or requested name.

A TCP/853 flow proves the switch is attempting DoT; it does not prove the server returned the intended record. A valid certificate proves the presented certificate chains to the configured CA; it does not prove the DNS zone is correct or that DNSSEC validation occurred. DoT is not DNSSEC. Likewise, a successful switch-originated lookup does not prove that client devices use the same resolver path.

Operational application

When migrating from cleartext, first confirm that both primary and secondary resolvers accept DoT and that intermediate firewalls permit TCP/853 from the switch's chosen source IP. Install the CA certificate before enabling validation. Test a known internal and external name, then test a negative name if negative caching is enabled. If the switch loses management-plane name resolution after the change, restore cleartext temporarily or correct the resolver path; do not disable certificate validation as a permanent workaround without a documented trust decision. The mechanism-to-implication rule is: protocol selection controls transport, CA configuration controls resolver identity, and source-IP/routing controls whether the management plane can reach the service at all.

lessons.title: BLE real-time location services: scan windows, tag filters and cloud reporting
lessons.mechanism: Managed FortiAP built-in Bluetooth radios scan BLE advertisers using a BLE profile; WTP profile binds the scan profile to an RTLS provider and sends filtered measurements to a cloud service.
lessons.workflow: BLE advertiser/tag -> AP scan window and RSSI threshold -> UUID/MAC allowlist -> accumulation/reporting interval -> WSS/TLS provider endpoint -> location analytics.
lessons.failure: Tags are visible over the air but absent from cloud analytics because scan profile is not applied, RSSI threshold excludes them, UUID/MAC filters do not match, or token/FQDN/egress is wrong.
lessons.evidence: wlac wtpprof proves controller profile and RTLS binding; cw_diag ble-config proves AP received scan settings; cw_diag ble-rtls proves endpoint/protocol settings, not cloud acceptance or location accuracy.
lessons.remediation: Tune scan type/window/threshold, bind BLE profile to WTP profile, verify provider endpoint/token and allowlists, then compare AP-side sightings with cloud ingestion.
lessons.diagram: BLE tag advertising to FortiAP scanner, filtering/aggregation and secure RTLS cloud reporting.
lessons.content_html:
FortiOS WiFi Controller supports BLE-based Real-Time Location Services for Pole Star and Evresys. A managed FortiAP uses its built-in Bluetooth radio to scan nearby BLE asset tags. The AP forwards selected observations to the configured RTLS cloud service, where the provider processes measurements and produces asset-location analytics. This is a different telemetry path from Wi-Fi client association: a BLE tag does not need to join the SSID, complete 802.1X, or obtain an IP address for its advertisements to be observed.

Scan profile mechanics

Create a BLE profile under config wireless-controller ble-profile. The profile enables scanning and controls whether the AP scans actively or passively. Active scanning sends a scan request to an advertiser for additional information; passive scanning only receives advertisements. The profile also controls scan-period, scan-time, scan-interval, scan-window and scan-threshold. The threshold is an RSSI floor from -95 to -20 dBm; the documented default is -90 dBm. A tag below the configured threshold can be heard intermittently by another receiver yet never be reported by this AP. The interval and window determine how much time the Bluetooth link layer listens on a channel, so they influence detection opportunity and reporting cadence.

config wireless-controller ble-profile
    edit "asset-tags"
        set ble-scanning enable
        set scan-type passive
        set scan-period 1000
        set scan-interval 30
        set scan-window 30
        set scan-threshold -90
    next
end

After creating the BLE profile, apply it to the FortiAP WTP profile. The WTP profile's config lbs section selects the provider and configures the server FQDN, path, access token, port, protocol, accumulation interval, reporting interval and asset filters. The provider can be Pole Star or Evresys. WSS is the documented default reporting protocol and the default port is 443. The guide supports filtering by asset UUID lists and by a firewall address group containing BLE tag MAC addresses; an address group can contain individual MAC addresses or ranges.

Measurement pipeline

The AP first hears the advertisement during a scan window. The configured scan threshold determines whether the AP reports the detected device. The RTLS profile then limits which UUIDs or MAC addresses are sent. Measurements are accumulated for the configured interval and reported at the reporting interval to the provider endpoint. This means there are several independent gates: RF reception, RSSI threshold, profile application, tag allowlist, provider token and endpoint reachability. A failure at any gate can look like “the tag is not on the map,” but each requires a different fix.

Verification: what each command proves

diagnose wireless-controller wlac -c wtpprof
# On the FortiAP:
cw_diag -c ble-config
cw_diag -c ble-rtls

wlac -c wtpprof shows the controller's WTP profile, BLE profile and RTLS provider settings. cw_diag -c ble-config shows that the AP received BLE scan configuration, including mode, threshold, period, time, interval and window. cw_diag -c ble-rtls shows the AP's provider type, protocol, FQDN, path and reporting parameters. These commands prove configuration propagation and local state. They do not prove that the cloud accepted the token, that the provider ingested every measurement, or that the location algorithm has enough AP observations for accurate positioning.

Operational troubleshooting

If no tags appear, start with one known tag close to one AP and temporarily use a permissive but safe RSSI threshold. Confirm passive or active mode matches the tag behavior, and check that the UUID or MAC address is in an enabled allowlist. If the AP sees the tag but the provider does not, verify the RTLS FQDN, path, token, TCP/443 egress and the selected WSS protocol. Compare accumulation and reporting intervals with the expected freshness of the map. If one AP reports but another does not, compare profile assignment and RF conditions before changing cloud settings. If all APs report but the map is inaccurate, inspect AP placement and overlapping observation coverage; the CLI's successful configuration output is not a location-accuracy test.

For deployment, keep provider tokens out of ordinary configuration exports and restrict who can edit WTP profiles. The design implication is that BLE location is a telemetry pipeline: radio scanning creates observations, filtering selects identities, batching controls freshness, and the RTLS provider turns multi-AP observations into location estimates. Troubleshoot each stage independently rather than treating the map as a single black box.

lessons.title: Kerberos authentication scope in FortiNAC 9.4: admin and user login are different support planes
lessons.mechanism: FortiNAC 9.4 adds Kerberos for administrator and user authentication on FortiNAC-CA, and administrator authentication on FNAC-M; the supported roles differ by platform.
lessons.workflow: Client/domain context -> Kerberos KDC ticket exchange -> FortiNAC authentication endpoint -> local application authorization; separate this from LDAP lookup, RADIUS endpoint access and machine domain join.
lessons.failure: Repeated admin/user login prompt despite directory reachability because realm, clock, service identity or ticket negotiation is wrong; unsupported platform/authentication scope is assumed.
lessons.evidence: KDC AS/TGS events and FortiNAC authentication logs show ticket issuance/validation path; successful LDAP search or TGT acquisition alone does not prove application authorization.
lessons.remediation: Confirm 9.4+ release and platform/scope first; validate DNS, time, realm and service identity using the version-matched guide; do not reuse another Fortinet product's Kerberos CLI blindly.
lessons.diagram: Client/KDC ticket exchange followed by FortiNAC application authentication and separate authorization decision.
lessons.content_html:
FortiNAC 9.4.0 adds Kerberos support, but the release note defines a deliberately narrow support matrix: Kerberos is supported for administrator and user authentication on FortiNAC-CA, and for administrator authentication on FNAC-M. Do not generalize that statement into “all FortiNAC logins on every appliance use Kerberos.” In particular, the release note does not state that FNAC-M user authentication is covered. That boundary should be part of the design and the troubleshooting checklist.

Where Kerberos fits

Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol. In a standard domain flow, the client obtains a Ticket-Granting Ticket from the Key Distribution Center (KDC), then requests a service ticket for the target service identity. The service validates the ticket using its configured service credentials and the KDC's trust context. The user's password is not sent to the FortiNAC service as a reusable cleartext password. This is different from an LDAP bind, where the application connects to a directory for a user lookup or bind; different again from RADIUS, which is commonly used to authenticate network access; and different from Winbind machine-domain join, which establishes a host's relationship with a directory domain.

The FortiNAC 9.4.0 New Features section is the authoritative source for the product-specific support scope. It does not publish a full SPN/keytab configuration sequence in that release-note entry. Therefore, do not copy a Kerberos configuration from FortiAuthenticator, FortiPAM, or another Fortinet product and assume the field names, service identity or supported encryption types are identical. Use the version-matched FortiNAC administration documentation for the actual deployment settings.

Prerequisites and transaction boundaries

At the protocol layer, Kerberos depends on accurate time, working DNS, correct realm naming, a reachable KDC and a service identity that matches the ticket requested by the client. A client may be domain joined and able to obtain a TGT while still failing to obtain a service ticket for the FortiNAC endpoint. A valid service ticket can also be accepted while the application subsequently denies access because the account lacks the required administrator or user role. Authentication and authorization are separate decisions.

For a change plan, record the exact FortiNAC platform (CA or FNAC-M), version, login class (administrator or user), domain/realm, DNS resolvers, time source and KDC reachability. Test one administrator account first. Only after that path succeeds should you test the user-authentication path on FortiNAC-CA. Do not infer user-authentication support on FNAC-M from an administrator login test.

Evidence-led troubleshooting

Correlate the FortiNAC authentication event with KDC events for the same user and timestamp. A KDC record showing a TGT was issued proves the client reached the KDC and authenticated to the realm; it does not prove the service ticket was issued for the correct FortiNAC service identity. A service-ticket failure directs attention to service identity/SPN registration, realm mapping, clock skew and encryption compatibility. If the KDC shows successful ticket issuance but FortiNAC denies the login, inspect the application authentication log and authorization/role mapping rather than repeatedly changing the user's password.

If LDAP lookup succeeds but the Kerberos login loops, do not treat LDAP reachability as proof that Kerberos is healthy. If the KDC is unreachable, check routing, firewall rules and DNS before changing FortiNAC. If only one appliance class fails, verify that the authentication type is in the 9.4 support matrix. If the ticket validates but the account is rejected, investigate the application role separately. Because the public release-note entry does not document every FortiNAC-specific configuration field, the honest operational boundary is to verify the product's version-specific settings instead of inventing CLI commands. This lesson is about understanding the supported authentication plane and the evidence needed to isolate it.

lessons.title: FortiGate VDOM multi-tenancy with FortiNAC-F: shared access hardware, separate tenant enforcement
lessons.mechanism: FortiGate MGMT/root VDOM manages shared FortiSwitch/FortiAP infrastructure while tenant VDOMs own tenant VLANs/SSIDs; FortiNAC-F maps each virtual device's logical networks to the VLANs in that VDOM.
lessons.workflow: FortiLink-managed switch -> export physical port to tenant VDOM -> create tenant VLAN/default VLAN -> VDOM-link routes/policies -> FortiNAC virtual-device and logical-network mapping -> endpoint VLAN assignment.
lessons.failure: Port appears only in root, tenant VLAN is created in wrong VDOM, DHCP relay/VDOM-link policy is missing, or FortiNAC maps a logical network to the wrong tenant VLAN.
lessons.evidence: Exported port is greyed in root and visible in tenant; FortiNAC Virtualized Devices lists root and tenant VDOMs; these prove control-plane mapping, not end-to-end DHCP or tenant reachability.
lessons.remediation: Verify FortiLink, exported port, tenant VLAN, VDOM link routes and firewall policies, DHCP relay, and per-VDOM FortiNAC Model Configuration; test a host in each tenant.
lessons.diagram: Shared root/MGMT FortiGate and FortiLink switch/AP with two tenant VDOMs, exported ports, VDOM links and separate logical VLANs.
lessons.content_html:
FortiNAC-F 7.6.5 supports a multi-tenant FortiGate design in which FortiGate, FortiSwitch and FortiAP provide shared physical infrastructure while each tenant receives a separate logical security domain. The MGMT/root VDOM is the highest security zone and manages the FortiLink switch and APs. Tenant VDOMs own their VLANs and can own SSIDs that are assigned to APs managed from the root VDOM. FortiNAC-F identifies the VDOM associated with a connected port and selects the VLAN in that VDOM according to the virtual-device settings.

Control-plane and forwarding architecture

Start with a FortiSwitch managed by FortiLink from the root/MGMT VDOM. A physical switch port can be exported into a tenant VDOM. The port is then managed by that tenant and can be assigned to a tenant VLAN. The tenant VDOM's VLAN interfaces remain separate from the root VDOM's VLANs. A VDOM link connects the tenant VDOM to root; tenant-to-external traffic, including traffic to FortiNAC, traverses the link and can be restricted by firewall policies in both VDOMs. This is not simply a shared switch with separate VLAN names: the VDOM ownership of the port, VLAN interface, routing and policy path must agree.

The integration guide's example creates a VLAN interface attached to fortilink, assigns it to the tenant VDOM, sets a VLAN ID and optionally configures DHCP relay to the FortiNAC interface. The default virtual-switch VLAN is then set in the tenant VDOM. From the root VDOM, the managed FortiSwitch port is exported with set export-to "<tenant VDOM>". In the root VDOM's switch-port view, the exported port appears greyed out; in the tenant VDOM, it is visible and can be managed there.

config system interface
    edit "traffic-iso"
        set vdom "traffic"
        set interface "fortilink"
        set vlanid 21
        set ip 10.10.21.1 255.255.255.0
        set dhcp-relay-service enable
        set dhcp-relay-ip 192.168.2.2
    next
end

config switch-controller global
    set default-virtual-switch-vlan "traffic-iso"
end

# In the root VDOM, on the managed FortiSwitch:
config ports
    edit "<port-to-export>"
        set export-to "traffic"
    next
end

Firewall and FortiNAC mapping

The tenant VDOM needs policies between tenant VLANs and the VDOM link. The root VDOM needs policies between the VDOM link and external interfaces, including the FortiNAC-facing interface. Static routes must provide the return path. The example guide shows separate policies in both VDOMs; a one-way policy is not enough for a bidirectional registration, DHCP relay or management transaction. If FortiNAC provides DHCP for an isolation VLAN, create the corresponding isolation scope in the FortiNAC configuration wizard.

Once FortiGate is connected to FortiNAC, open Network > Inventory > Virtualized Devices. The root VDOM and tenant VDOM should both be visible. Select the tenant VDOM and open Model Configuration. Map logical networks such as Registration, remediation and production to VLANs that exist in that tenant VDOM. The example maps Registration to VLAN 21 and production to VLAN 22. Repeat the mapping for each tenant; do not reuse a VLAN ID assumption across VDOMs without checking the actual interface ownership.

Verification and failure isolation

Validate in layers. First confirm FortiSwitch is managed by FortiLink and the port is exported to the intended tenant. Second confirm the tenant VLAN interface is attached to the correct FortiLink interface and VDOM. Third confirm the VDOM link, routes and policies allow the required FortiNAC, DHCP and external traffic. Fourth confirm FortiNAC sees both virtualized devices and that each logical network maps to the VLAN in the correct tenant. Finally connect a test host in each tenant and verify registration, DHCP, gateway reachability and intended isolation.

A greyed-out port in root and a visible port in the tenant prove the export operation, not that DHCP or firewall policy works. A tenant VDOM appearing in FortiNAC proves device discovery, not that its logical networks map to the right VLANs. If the endpoint receives no address, inspect the DHCP relay path and isolation scope. If the endpoint receives an address but cannot reach FortiNAC, inspect VDOM-link policies and return routes. If a host lands in the wrong tenant VLAN, inspect the virtual-device mapping and exported-port ownership before changing the endpoint profile.

The documented compatibility baseline is FortiNAC-F 7.6.5+, FortiGate 7.2.9+ and FortiSwitch 7.2.0+; the guide calls out a FortiGate port-name update requirement for FortiGate 7.4.9 and later in the relevant integration steps. Treat the exact release combination as part of the design. The security implication is that shared physical infrastructure does not imply shared tenant forwarding: the VDOM boundary, port export, VLAN mapping and firewall policy must all preserve the intended separation.

lessons.title: FortiGuest guest portals in FortiAuthenticator 8.0: hosted pages, rules and beta boundaries
lessons.mechanism: FortiAuthenticator 8.0 embeds FortiGuest portal configuration through Portals, Portals Rules and Guest Themes; rules select a hosted portal, while authentication is limited to local users in the beta.
lessons.workflow: Client captive-portal redirect -> FortiAuthenticator hosted portal -> portal-rule evaluation -> local-user authentication -> success/failure response -> network gateway continues its access workflow.
lessons.failure: Portal renders but user cannot authenticate, wrong portal is selected, theme customization is lost after restore, or HA is assumed to support the beta feature.
lessons.evidence: Portal preview proves page rendering; rule match proves portal selection; local authentication logs prove credential validation; none proves gateway VLAN/role enforcement.
lessons.remediation: Validate redirect URL, portal rule order/conditions, local user state and gateway response; back up customizations separately and do not deploy the beta in unsupported HA.
lessons.diagram: Captive client redirect to FortiAuthenticator portal, rule selector, local-user authentication and gateway return path.
lessons.content_html:
FortiAuthenticator 8.0.0 introduces FortiGuest features inside FortiAuthenticator through a Guest Portals (beta) menu under Authentication. The feature exposes three distinct configuration areas: Portals, where administrators create and host portal pages; Portals Rules, where administrators create rules that direct users to different portals; and Guest Themes, where portal presentation is customized. This is not merely a theme editor. It adds a portal-hosting and portal-selection layer to the authentication appliance.

Request and decision flow

In a typical captive-portal deployment, a client joins a guest network and the network gateway redirects the browser to the configured portal host. FortiAuthenticator serves the portal page. The portal-rule layer determines which configured portal should be presented for the request, based on the rule conditions and their evaluation context. The user then authenticates against the supported identity source. For this beta, Fortinet documents local-user login only. After successful authentication, the portal returns the success path expected by the network gateway, which continues its own access-control workflow. Keep the components separate: FortiAuthenticator hosts and authenticates the portal; the gateway still controls the network session, VLAN, firewall policy or captive-portal release.

Portal rules are the policy-selection layer. A page that renders successfully does not prove that the intended rule matched, and a rule match does not prove that the user authenticated. A successful local login does not prove that the gateway accepted the return transaction or assigned the expected access. During design, document the redirect destination, portal selection conditions, local-user realm, success/failure behavior and the gateway's expected completion path.

Configuration and operational boundaries

Build the portal page first, then define the portal rules that select it, then apply the required guest theme. Test each portal with a known local account and with a request that should match a different rule. Use a default or fallback portal deliberately rather than relying on an accidental first match. Keep the portal hostname and certificate consistent with the captive-portal redirect so browsers do not fail before the login page is displayed.

Fortinet explicitly marks Guest Portals as beta and documents four limitations: only local users are supported for login; configuration backup/restore does not preserve all customizations; HA active-passive and active-active are not supported; and only administrators with full permissions can access the configuration. These limitations are architectural, not cosmetic. Do not deploy this feature on an HA pair and assume the portal configuration will synchronize. Do not assume LDAP, RADIUS, SAML or external identity-provider login is supported simply because FortiAuthenticator supports those methods elsewhere. Do not treat a standard appliance backup as a complete archive of portal themes and customizations.

Evidence and troubleshooting

Test the flow in stages. First browse directly to the portal host and confirm the page and theme render. Next generate a captive redirect and verify that the request lands on the intended portal. Then test a valid and invalid local user. Finally verify that the network gateway receives the expected success or failure response and changes the client session accordingly. If the page is wrong, inspect portal-rule conditions and selection order. If the page is correct but login fails, inspect the local account state and authentication logs. If login succeeds but the client remains in the registration network, inspect the gateway's captive-portal response handling and VLAN/session policy; changing the portal theme will not fix that path.

For recovery, preserve portal definitions, rules and themes using the supported export or manual capture process appropriate to the installed build, and test the restore process in a non-HA lab. The documentation warns that backup/restore does not preserve all customizations, so the runbook must include a separate theme and page recovery plan. The safe operational conclusion is to treat this as a beta, local-user-only portal feature with explicit HA and backup constraints, not as a drop-in replacement for a fully supported external guest identity architecture.

lessons.title: SSH command filtering: parser semantics, restricted mode and the audit trail
lessons.mechanism: FortiPAM parses SSH shell input into command and parameters, evaluates simple/exact/regex patterns, and applies deny-list or restricted allow-list semantics to the secret's SSH launcher.
lessons.workflow: Create SSH filter profile -> select Deny or Allow/restricted mode -> add patterns and log/severity settings -> attach profile to SSH-enabled secret -> evaluate each command/channel -> write SSH Filter Log.
lessons.failure: An administrator expects a prefix rule to match only one parameter set, assumes Deny mode is an allowlist, or forgets that owner bypass and non-shell channels are separate controls.
lessons.evidence: SSH Filter Log shows Blocked or Passthrough and command metadata; it proves filter action, not the full target-side impact or that every non-shell channel is blocked.
lessons.remediation: Test exact and prefix patterns, compound commands, regex fallback, channels and owner bypass with a non-production secret; audit legacy Action=Allow entries after upgrade.
lessons.diagram: SSH launcher input parser, simple/exact/regex match stages, deny/restricted decision, channel controls and audit log.
lessons.content_html:
FortiPAM SSH filter profiles enforce command-level controls for SSH launcher sessions. The profile is attached to a secret, so the control follows the privileged connection to the target rather than relying only on a user's terminal discipline. The critical detail is parser behavior: FortiPAM does not treat the entire typed line as one opaque string. It parses the shell input into a command and parameters, then evaluates configured patterns. A policy that looks correct in the GUI can therefore be broader or narrower than the operator intended.

Deny mode and restricted mode

Deny mode is the legacy block-list model: configured patterns are commands the user may not execute. Allow mode is restricted mode: configured patterns are commands the user may execute, and other inputs are blocked. The CLI exposes the mode through set restricted-mode disable for deny mode and set restricted-mode enable for restricted/allow mode. Do not confuse a pattern whose action is Allow inside a Deny-mode profile with the new restricted mode; the legacy pattern action can permit and log a specific command without blocking all other commands.

Pattern types matter. “Start with single word” parses a line such as ifconfig eth0 down into command ifconfig and parameters eth0 down. A pattern for ifconfig therefore matches any shell input beginning with that command. If the goal is to block only ifconfig eth0 down while allowing ifconfig virbr0 up, use Exact Match. Regular-expression patterns provide a more expressive final match, but they should be tested against the exact shell strings the target accepts.

Compound commands and evaluation

FortiPAM documents compound input separated by semicolons and ampersands. For a line such as date; ls -l; rm /home/folder/sensitive/docs, the parser evaluates each command against the simple patterns first. If a simple pattern matches in Deny mode, the sentence is blocked. If no simple pattern matches, regex patterns are checked. In restricted mode, each command must match an allowed pattern; if one command cannot be matched, the compound line is blocked. This prevents an allowed command from being used as a wrapper around a prohibited second command, but it also means operators must test shell grouping and separators used by their target environments.

SSH profiles also control channels such as X11, SSH exec, port forwarding, tunnel forwarding, SFTP, SCP and unknown channels. A shell-command pattern is not a substitute for channel restrictions. Configure those channel blocks independently. The profile can log individual patterns, set severity and send alerts; “Log All Unlisted Commands” changes the audit volume and should be chosen deliberately.

Apply and verify

config ssh-filter profile
    edit "ops-restricted"
        set restricted-mode enable
        set shortcut-input enable
        config shell-commands
            edit 1
                set pattern "show"
                set type simple
                set log enable
            next
            edit 2
                set pattern "show system status"
                set exact-match enable
                set log enable
            next
        end
    next
end

In the GUI, create the profile under Secret Settings > SSH Filter Profiles. Then open the target secret under Secrets > Secrets, enable SSH Service, enable SSH Filter, select the profile and save. The filter does not apply merely because the profile exists; it must be attached to the secret used by the launcher.

After a test session, inspect the SSH Filter Log. It records the command and whether the action was Blocked or Passthrough, along with user, secret and destination context in the SSH logs. A Blocked event proves the filter stopped that command at the FortiPAM control point. A Passthrough event proves the command was permitted by the filter; it does not prove the target command succeeded. If video recording is enabled, correlate the event with the session video for user-visible context.

Migration and bypass caveats

Fortinet documents a legacy-upgrade trap: profiles upgraded from FortiPAM 1.3.0 or below may contain Action=Allow entries that are not displayed in the new pattern table. Those entries do not block other commands; the new Allow/restricted mode does. Inspect the CLI configuration during migration rather than assuming the GUI list is complete. Also review “Bypass for owner” on the secret: when enabled, the secret owner can bypass commands that the filter would otherwise prohibit. The safe pattern is to test a non-production secret with benign and prohibited commands, compound separators, SFTP/SCP and port-forward channels, then verify the resulting logs before applying the profile to production privileged accounts.

lessons.title: Maintenance Calendars: suppress monitoring noise without hiding the scope of a change
lessons.mechanism: A calendar schedule gates performance, availability and change monitoring/rule triggers for selected devices and Synthetic Transaction Monitoring tasks during a defined maintenance interval.
lessons.workflow: Create calendar -> define one-time or recurring time range -> select devices/groups and STM tasks -> optionally enable incident generation during maintenance -> calendar view and incident behavior.
lessons.failure: A maintenance window suppresses too many devices or the wrong STM tasks; an operator assumes raw event ingestion or all security detection is disabled.
lessons.evidence: Calendar view and selected scope prove schedule configuration; missing performance/availability/change incidents during the window are expected; they do not prove raw logs stopped ingesting.
lessons.remediation: Scope devices and STM tasks explicitly, validate recurrence/time range and optional incident override, and compare the calendar with change tickets and device-group membership.
lessons.diagram: Calendar schedule and device/STM scope gating monitoring and rule generation with optional incident override.
lessons.content_html:
FortiSIEM Maintenance Calendars reduce alert noise during planned work by marking selected devices and Synthetic Transaction Monitoring (STM) tasks as under maintenance for a defined interval. The documented behavior is specific: while a device is in maintenance, FortiSIEM does not monitor it for performance, availability and change, and the corresponding rules do not trigger. This is a monitoring/rule-suppression control, not a blanket “stop collecting security data” switch.

Objects and scope

A Maintenance Calendar has a required name, optional description, schedule and a selection of device groups/devices and STM tasks. The schedule defines a time range (start time and duration) and a recurrence pattern. The guide supports a one-time date, recurring days of the week and recurring months, with a start/end recurrence range or no end date for an ongoing schedule. The scope selector separates Devices from STM tasks, so an operator can suppress a synthetic test without suppressing every device in the same network, or select a group when the entire group is undergoing work.

To create one, go to ADMIN > Setup > Maintenance, select New, provide the name and schedule, then choose the devices/groups and STM tasks. There is an optional setting, “Generate Incidents for Devices under Maintenance.” When enabled, it changes the default suppression behavior for incidents during the maintenance window. It should be an explicit decision, not a checkbox left to chance.

What the calendar does—and does not do

The supported statement is that performance, availability and change monitoring are suppressed for selected devices and the corresponding rules do not trigger during maintenance. Do not extend that statement to raw event ingestion, every correlation rule, or every security event type unless the specific rule and data path are documented. A firewall may still send logs while its availability monitor is suppressed. A security incident may still be created if the optional “Generate Incidents” behavior is enabled or if another data source/rule is not covered by the maintenance scope. The calendar is not a substitute for a firewall policy, log filter or ingestion pause.

This distinction is important for incident triage. If a device is quiet in the performance dashboard during maintenance, that may be expected. If its raw logs disappear, investigate the collector, event transport and ingestion path separately. If an incident appears during the window, check whether the incident-generation override is enabled and whether the rule is actually one of the performance/availability/change rules affected by the calendar.

Verification and failure isolation

FortiSIEM provides month, week/list and day views, plus a Current view for active maintenance. Use these views to confirm the window is active at the time of the change. Verify the selected devices and STM tasks in the calendar definition, not just the human-readable description. A calendar named “Core network maintenance” may still include a broader device group than the change ticket intended. After saving, compare the selected scope with the change record and test a known monitored device that should remain outside the window.

Common failures are schedule errors, scope errors and assumptions about what is suppressed. A recurring monthly schedule can extend beyond the change window if the recurrence end date is omitted. A device group may gain new members after the calendar is created, changing the practical blast radius. A synthetic transaction may remain active if it was not selected under STM. Conversely, selecting a broad group can hide a real outage on a device that was not part of the planned work. Use explicit groups or device lists and review membership before each recurring window.

For operational governance, link each calendar to a change ticket, owner, start/end time and rollback condition. Keep a test device outside the calendar to prove the monitoring pipeline remains active. After maintenance, verify that monitoring resumes and that delayed alerts are evaluated according to the product's rule behavior. The key implication is that a Maintenance Calendar changes observability for a selected scope and time interval; it does not make the underlying infrastructure healthy, nor does it prove that every event source stopped reporting.

lessons.title: Secure Private Access application monitoring: PoP-originated ICMP probes to private apps
lessons.mechanism: FortiSASE Security PoPs initiate ICMP health checks every second to up to 20 custom private IPv4 applications hosted behind SPA Hubs; SLA thresholds are evaluated per PoP and SPA Hub service connection.
lessons.workflow: Define application name/private IPv4 -> set latency/jitter/loss targets -> PoP probes through SPA service connection -> SLA failure view -> per-PoP drilldown history.
lessons.failure: ICMP is blocked or routed differently from application TCP/TLS traffic; one PoP or hub path fails while the application remains healthy for user traffic, or thresholds are too tight.
lessons.evidence: SLA Failure tab shows measured latency/jitter/loss per PoP and hub connection; it proves ICMP probe behavior, not HTTP/TLS/authentication or transaction success.
lessons.remediation: Permit/validate ICMP probe path, compare per-PoP and per-hub results, set thresholds from baseline, and pair ICMP monitoring with an application-layer synthetic test.
lessons.diagram: FortiSASE Security PoPs sending ICMP probes through SPA hubs to private application servers with per-PoP SLA comparison.
lessons.content_html:
FortiSASE Secure Private Access (SPA) application monitoring is a targeted observability feature for private applications hosted behind SPA Hubs. The documented limit is up to 20 custom applications. Fortinet Security PoPs initiate ICMP health-check probes to each defined application every second. Administrators set latency, jitter and packet-loss thresholds, then view the measured values by Security PoP and SPA Hub service connection. This is not the same measurement as a user's browser transaction or a generic public-SaaS availability test; the probe target is a private application behind the SPA architecture.

Configuration objects and measurement path

Open Operations > Connectivity > Digital Experience Monitoring and select the SPA application monitoring tab. Under Settings, create a custom application with a name and a valid private IPv4 address for the application server. Enable the required SLA targets and define latency, jitter and packet-loss thresholds. The application object represents the private server being monitored; the service connection and Security PoP provide the path context for the measurement.

Each PoP originates an ICMP probe every second. The probe traverses the SPA service connection toward the defined private application. The platform records latency, jitter and packet loss and compares them with the configured thresholds. In the SLA Failure tab, actual values are arranged by Security PoP against the configured SPA Hub service connections. Selecting a PoP and using Drilldown exposes historical values. This per-PoP view is useful because a single private server may be reachable through one PoP/hub path and impaired through another.

What the measurement proves

A successful ICMP probe proves that the probe source can reach the target using the ICMP path that the monitoring service uses. It does not prove that the application listens on TCP/443, that a TLS handshake succeeds, that SSO works, that the user is authorized, or that a specific HTTP transaction completes. Conversely, a failed ICMP probe does not always prove the application is down: a firewall may block ICMP while allowing the application's TCP port, or a device may rate-limit ICMP differently from application traffic. Treat the SLA as a network reachability/quality signal, not an application transaction test.

Thresholds also need a baseline. A latency threshold that is too low can create persistent false failures on a naturally long path. A packet-loss threshold that is too high can mask a real degradation. Establish a baseline from normal operating periods and compare per-PoP behavior. If all PoPs fail at once, suspect the application server, its local firewall or the common SPA hub/service connection. If one PoP fails while others remain healthy, investigate the PoP-to-hub route, regional path or service-connection state before restarting the application.

Operational troubleshooting

When a dashboard reports an SLA failure, identify the failing PoP and hub connection first. Compare latency, jitter and loss against the configured targets and the historical drilldown. Confirm that the private IPv4 address is correct and that the server responds to ICMP from the SPA monitoring path. If ICMP is intentionally blocked, do not simply lower the threshold or mark the app healthy; document the limitation and use a separate application-layer synthetic check for the user experience.

Use a two-layer monitoring design: SPA ICMP monitoring to detect path and reachability changes, plus an application-aware test that checks the actual service port, TLS certificate, authentication and a representative request. If ICMP is healthy but users cannot log in, investigate the application transaction, identity provider and policy. If ICMP is unhealthy but the application works, validate the probe policy and decide whether ICMP should be allowed. The uniqueness of this feature is the private-app target and PoP-to-SPA-Hub measurement path; it should not be conflated with public SaaS DEM or endpoint-to-PoP TCP latency measurements.

lessons.title: L3 VPN segmentation over a single multi-VRF IPsec overlay
lessons.mechanism: A single IPsec overlay carries multiple VRF contexts using VPN-ID/IPIP encapsulation; BGP CE/PE VRF roles, RD and route-target import/export preserve route separation.
lessons.workflow: Configure tunnel encapsulation -> define VRFs/RDs/RTs -> exchange routes per VRF -> run VRF-aware health checks -> keep hub egress on the ingress overlay when SLA is met.
lessons.failure: Traffic leaks between tenants, route is absent in one VRF, health check runs in the wrong VRF, or hub sends a flow out a different overlay than the ingress path.
lessons.evidence: VRF route tables and BGP RT/RD state prove control-plane separation; VRF-aware SLA output proves probe context; packet capture and policy counters prove forwarding path, not tenant authorization by themselves.
lessons.remediation: Verify VPN-ID encapsulation, matching VRF IDs, RD/RT import/export, source/VRF on health checks, route/policy symmetry and overlay tie-break behavior.
lessons.diagram: Hub-and-spoke IPsec overlay with VRF-A and VRF-B encapsulated over one tunnel, separate route tables and VRF-aware SLA probes.
lessons.content_html:
FortiOS 8.0 documents L3 VPN segmentation over a single overlay. The design allows multiple VRF contexts to use one IPsec overlay rather than building a separate physical or tunnel overlay for every tenant. The separation is carried in the tunnel encapsulation and preserved by the VRF routing context. This is not ordinary VLAN tagging and it is not route leaking between VRFs: the goal is to carry multiple isolated routing tables over shared tunnel infrastructure while allowing the same VRF to communicate across sites.

Encapsulation and route distribution

The IPsec phase-1 interface is configured for VPN-ID/IPIP encapsulation using set encapsulation vpn-id-ipip. The tunnel can then carry traffic associated with different VRFs. The VRF model uses CE/PE roles, route distinguishers and route targets. The RD makes routes unique in the VPN control plane; import/export route targets determine which VRFs accept which VPN routes. If the route target is wrong, the tunnel may be up and BGP may be established while a tenant route is absent from the intended VRF. If the wrong VRF is selected, the route can be present but isolated from the expected forwarding table.

On a hub, the same overlay interface can carry VRF-A and VRF-B traffic. Each VRF maintains its own route table and policy context. A site that hosts multiple tenants can therefore use one overlay transport while keeping tenant route distribution separate. The feature is especially useful where tunnel count and operational overhead matter, but it increases the importance of consistent VRF IDs, route targets and source addresses at every site.

VRF-aware health checks and path stickiness

SD-WAN health checks must probe from the correct VRF. The FortiOS guide exposes a VRF selection and source address for the health-check object. A probe launched in the default/global table may fail even when the tenant VRF has a working route, or may succeed over the wrong path and incorrectly mark the tenant overlay healthy. Bind the health check to the VRF that owns the application route and choose a source address in that VRF.

When a hub has multiple overlays, overlay stickiness can keep traffic received on one overlay from being forwarded out another overlay when the SLA is satisfied. The service tie-break options include input-device or input-zone behavior. This matters for symmetric forwarding, stateful inspection and tenant separation. Without the intended tie-break, the hub may receive a flow on one tunnel and send the return traffic through another overlay, producing asymmetric routing or an unexpected firewall path.

Configuration and verification approach

config vpn ipsec phase1-interface
    edit "overlay-shared"
        set encapsulation vpn-id-ipip
    next
end

config system sdwan
    config health-check
        edit "vrf-a-probe"
            set vrf 10
            set source 10.10.10.1
        next
    end
end

The snippet is illustrative: use the exact VRF IDs, source addresses and supported options for the installed FortiOS build. Verify the phase-1 encapsulation, the VRF objects and BGP route-target policy at both ends. Inspect each VRF route table and confirm that only the intended route targets are imported. Then check the health-check status in the same VRF and confirm that the probe source is reachable. Use SD-WAN service diagnostics and packet captures to validate the selected overlay and the actual ingress/egress interface.

Failure isolation and caveats

If the IPsec tunnel is up but a tenant route is missing, inspect BGP adjacency, route distinguisher and import/export route targets before rebuilding the tunnel. If the SLA is down while tenant traffic works, check the health-check VRF and source. If a hub forwards a flow over a different tunnel than it arrived on, inspect the SD-WAN service tie-break and input-device/input-zone settings. Confirm firewall policies and static routes in the relevant VDOM/VRF; an overlay route does not grant authorization by itself.

The guide notes that the multi-VRF IPsec overlay is for forwarding traffic and is not used for local-out traffic. Do not expect locally originated FortiGate traffic to use the same VRF-in-overlay path without a separate supported design. Test each tenant independently and include a negative test proving that VRF-A cannot reach VRF-B. The mechanism-to-implication chain is: VPN-ID encapsulation identifies the routing context, RD/RT controls route visibility, VRF-aware SLA tests the correct path, and overlay stickiness preserves the intended return path. A healthy tunnel alone proves none of those tenant-specific conditions.
